segments.text: The primary battle is over, and now the
race for Florida governor is officially
on. Republican Byron Donalds and
Democrat David Jolly have secured the
party nominations at this point. Donalds
is backed by President Donald Trump. He
pitched his vision to supporters last
night, promising to lower property
taxes, support school choice, and audit
state agencies. He emphasized that
despite the high-profile endorsement, he
is not taking anything for granted right
now.
>> You also have to get out there and see
the people yourself. You can't just sit
back and think that the president's
endorsement is going to carry you. I've
seen other people where that did not
work out, and the president knows this.
He and I had this conversation.
Um it was very clear. He's like, "You
have my endorsement. Now the real work
begins." And he was correct.
>> Meanwhile, David Jolly celebrated his
Democratic victory alongside running
mate Gwen Graham. The former Republican
congressman believes voters are looking
for a moderate alternative. He's
focusing on affordability, including
lower home insurance rates, expanding
Medicaid, and raising teacher pay.
>> And I will also tell you yes, as an
old-school Republican, I talk about
ending the culture wars not to celebrate
some progressive platform, but because I
still believe in the old-school
Republican libertarian policy that
government SHOULD SIMPLY STAY OUT OF
YOUR LIFE and stay out OF YOUR BEDROOM,
AND STAY OUT OF YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE.
>> SO, let's talk more about it right now.
David Jolly joins us live here on Good
Day Orlando Extra this morning.
Congratulations. Great to see you,
David. Appreciate your time today.
>> Thank you. Good to be with you. Thank
you.
>> Let's go back in time here. You used to
be Republican. I think that's the last
time I interviewed you, but now a
Democrat. Now, for people who don't know
your political story, why did you change
parties? What's your backstory there?
>> Yeah, and I would point out I spent 7
years as an independent, one of the most
informative times of my life, being
untethered from major party dogma,
thinking about big problems that need
big solutions. Look, I was kind of a
Bush 41 Republican who fought the Tea
Party, fought Trumpism, and lost. But
I'll tell you this, I found my home in
today's Democratic Party because of
three basic values that I've always
tried to exercise. I think economic
growth is good. Florida's economy should
continue to grow, but it's got to grow
for everybody. I'm a capitalist. We
should lead with the private sector, but
the truth is government has to step in
and help out in some spaces. Housing,
healthcare, education, clean water,
clean air, safe communities. And then as
you heard in that sound, you know, I do
take the less government approach, the
true less government approach, the true
trust people with their personal freedom
approach. Stay out of their life, their
doctor's office, their bedroom. I'm in a
very post-ideological space in my career
where I think Florida's voters are just
looking for answers to their personal
economy and for a government to stay out
of their life.
>> Now, you know this, everybody knows
this. You now have to convince about a
million Florida voters to support you
because Republicans outnumber Democrats.
We know that. So, how do you convince
other people to follow you and support
you in this case?
>> You know, those voters aren't always
available to us as Democrats, but this
cycle they are. This cycle is one in
which voters are asking for change. In
'22, they were asking to stay the
course, but what we've seen in our
congressional special elections,
we've seen voters swing by 15 to 20
points for Democratic candidates. The
city of Miami elected a Democratic mayor
for the first time in 30 years. Voters
are begging for change. If Republicans
understood that, they would have
answers, but they don't. Listen, this
campaign is laser-focused on housing,
healthcare, and education. People say
there's affordability crisis. What does
that mean? The basic pillars of people's
personal economy. It shifts through the
generations, but can I stay in my home?
If I'm a homeowner, can you reduce my
interest rate? If I'm a renter, can I
live in the community in which I work?
Where does my family get healthcare and
is there a good public school in my
neighborhood that I can send my family
to? When I go out on the weekends, or is
the water clean? Is the air clean?
That's the basics. And so sure, Byron
Donalds is launching culture wars. He's
calling me radical. I said, "I'm not
radical. I'm not even cool." He's just
trying to make this a scary race where
we hate each other, where we're divided.
I'm saying, "Look, on the basics, we all
agree. Housing, healthcare, education.
That's it. That's what voters are asking
for and that's what we're building a
campaign to address."
>> I want to ask you very quickly, one of
the ads that was running said that
uh you promised to apologize to the
world for Florida. Do you want to Do you
want to clarify that conversation, what
happened there?
>> I think our culture wars have offended
many people. We've marginalized
Floridians based on the color of their
skin, who they love, who they worship,
where they were born, and I think it's
wrong. Our tourist numbers have softened
because people are afraid to come to
Florida. They feel unwelcome. Our kids
and our grandkids are leaving the state
because they don't feel like Florida is
a place that embraces everybody. Yes,
look, I I am a person deeply rooted in
Christian faith. I believe in a faith
that says we extend grace and love to
everybody. But you don't have to
practice faith to believe in Jefferson's
natural rights of man. We should be a
state where everybody's empowered,
everybody's welcome, everybody is lifted
up, their dignity is respected. And so,
yes, I think it's wrong what Ron
DeSantis and Byron Donalds are doing to
the state, dividing us based on the
color of our skin, where we were born,
who we love, or who we worship. As
governor, I hope to apologize to the
international community that has stopped
coming, stopped bringing their
conventions, the tourists who have
stopped coming, the Canadians who have
stopped coming for snowbird season.
Listen, we should apologize for making
people feel unwelcome. I'm not going to
back down off of that.
>> All right. Once again, David Jolly, got
to stop it there to keep the time
consistent throughout all of our
interviews. We appreciate your time
today. I'm sure we'll speak very again
again soon very soon as we head to
November.
